content.text: Three weeks after the oath, the Light still answered Falanaras too quickly.

He called it into his sword as Theron advanced across the practice court. Red-gold fire ran from the crossguard to the point, thin at first, then bright enough to stain the black lacquer of his gauntlets. Theron’s shield came up. A matching radiance spread over its face in a curved plane.
Falanaras struck.

Steel met the shield with a crack that jarred both arms. The ward bowed inward. Theron slid half a pace across the flagstones and turned the blade aside. Falanaras let the motion carry him around, brought the pommel toward Theron’s temple, and found the shield rim waiting. Theron drove forward behind it. The blow caught Falanaras in the breastplate and sent him back hard enough to scrape sparks from one heel.
The Light surged in answer to his anger.

For one dangerous instant the whole length of the sword blazed. Hunger vanished from his body. The old ache behind his ribs disappeared so completely that relief became its own temptation. Beneath that sweetness ran another sensation: a high, broken vibration at the edge of hearing. M’uru’s pain trembled within every measure he took.
“Enough,” Liadrin said.

Falanaras closed the channel. The fire collapsed to a thread and went out. Theron lowered his shield, breathing through his nose. A pale line showed where the sword had bitten into the red-black enamel.

Around them, the other Blood Knights halted their exercises. Fourteen black-and-crimson figures stood across the court beneath Silvermoon’s early light. They had been soldiers, guards, rangers, and former servants of a faith that no longer held them. The new tabards made an order of them. Their mismatched armor still revealed how recently the order had been named.

Liadrin crossed the flagstones with her ranseur resting against one shoulder. Light moved beneath her eyes in faint gold currents, visible within the fel-green. The gold burned more brightly in her than in any of them. Her hand remained steady around the weapon.
“Why did you let anger increase the draw?” she asked.
“He had me off balance.”
“Then recover your balance. More force is not failure. Letting temper choose it is.”
Theron leaned on his shield. “I offered to wait.”
“You said I looked tired.” Falanaras kept his gaze on Liadrin. “It was phrased less generously.”
“You still look tired,” Theron repeated. “I stand by the diagnosis.”
A few of the knights smiled. Liadrin did not, though something in her expression eased.

“The Light will answer fear, pain, pride, and appetite,” she said. “That makes it useful in battle. It also makes every weakness in you a hand upon the channel. If you cannot tell need from impulse on a quiet court, you will fail when someone is dying beside you.”

Her gaze traveled across the order. “Use the force the task requires. Put it where it belongs. Hold it as long as command and purpose demand, then end it. Discipline is not timidity, and the Light does not exempt you from judgment because the current wears a sacred color.”

Falanaras felt the rebuke settle deeper than the dent Theron had put in his breastplate. He had heard the same lesson beneath Deatholme, when Rynel spent his last strength on the passage and the soldiers depending on him rather than on his own hunger. The source had changed. The danger had learned to shine.

Boots sounded beneath the archway. Lethira entered the court with rain darkening the shoulders of her ranger leathers and three Farstriders behind her. She looked over the scorched practice posts, the cracked shields, and the knights standing in ordered lines.
“I see the city has found a cheaper way to ruin training equipment.”
Theron glanced at his shield. “Cheaper remains unproven.”

Lethira’s answering look held the old familiarity. The strain beneath it was newer. Mud streaked one boot to the knee, and the fletching at her shoulder had been tied down for hard riding. She carried a sealed message tube in one hand.

She offered the tube to Liadrin. “Halduron’s report. Amani war bands have moved west of Zul’Aman in strength. They struck two southern watch posts, left one burning, and broke every Scourge fetish they found along the Dead Scar.”
Liadrin broke the seal. “Driving the undead before them.”

“That is the assumption. Our southern riders lost the trail in the blight. The runestone wardens felt three impacts against the boundary before dawn.” Lethira’s mouth tightened. “The last one was larger.”

The court went silent. Beyond its walls, Silvermoon’s ward-lamps hummed and market awnings snapped in the wet wind. Three weeks of training had given the Blood Knights a uniform, a doctrine, and wounds earned beneath controlled ceilings. None had yet carried M’uru’s Light beyond the city.
Liadrin rolled the message shut. “Mount within the hour.”
They rode south under a sky the color of old steel.

Hawkstrider claws tore at the rain-soft road. The Blood Knights traveled in two files behind Liadrin, black cloaks lifting over crimson saddlecloths. Lethira’s Farstriders ranged ahead and along the flanks, appearing between copper-barked trees before vanishing into the enchanted green. Eversong held perpetual spring again, yet the restored runestones could not erase the scars beneath it. New grass covered old trenches. Pale sap bled from trunks split by siege fire years before.

Falanaras rode near the front with his two-handed sword secured across his back. No shield burdened him. He had tried one during the first week and learned what Theron had known for years: protection required a patience different from endurance. Falanaras’s instincts drove him toward the spellcaster behind the line, the ward holding a gate, the hand directing the blade. Theron preferred to become the obstacle those threats could not pass.

They had built the order’s first field doctrine from such differences. Some knights learned to hold overlapping barriers. Others turned Light through heavy weapons or carried it into wounds. Every exercise ended with Liadrin demanding an accounting: how much power, for what result, and what remained after the need had passed.
The questions had sounded severe in Silvermoon. South of the city, with smoke staining the horizon, they became practical.

Near midday they passed the first watch post. The tower still stood, though its lower room had burned. Two rangers lay beneath cloaks beside the road. A third sat against a runestone marker while a healer wrapped his forearm. He watched the Blood Knights pass with a ranger’s habitual suspicion sharpened by pain.

One of the knights broke formation and dismounted. She knelt beside him, laid two fingers above the soaked bandage, and drew a narrow current. Red-gold radiance entered the wound. The ranger gasped. Torn flesh closed beneath the cloth, enough to slow the bleeding and restore movement without hiding the damage entirely.
The Light withdrew. The knight swayed once when she stood.
The ranger flexed his hand. Distrust remained in his face. So did wonder.
“You can thank the naaru when we return,” Lethira said from the saddle.
The wounded ranger looked between her and the knight. He seemed unsure whether she had made a joke. Falanaras was unsure as well.

They pressed on. The air changed by degrees. Spring warmth thinned. Birdsong failed. The golden leaves nearest the southern boundary curled inward despite the rain, and every active runestone carried a faint pressure against Falanaras’s spellbreaker senses. The network was holding something away. Each mile made that resistance more urgent.

Theron rode beside him. When the tremor entered Falanaras’s fingers, he admitted a measured thread of Light. Relief moved through him at once, warm and complete, with M’uru’s broken music beneath it. He closed the draw while more remained. Theron watched his hand settle and said nothing until the current was gone.
“Better?” Theron asked.
“Adequate.”
“A stirring endorsement.”
Ahead, Lethira raised a fist.

The column slowed. A lone figure stood where the road bent around a fractured runestone. Hood down, bow held across her body, she wore the dark leather and black fletching of Sylvanas’s rangers. Rain silvered the gray skin at her temples. A narrow scar divided one dead eyebrow.
Serenya Duskrunner waited on the northern side of the boundary.
Lethira’s hand lowered to the hilt of her long knife. The motion appeared unconscious. Serenya saw it and gave no sign.
“You are late,” the dark ranger said.
“You are north of the line,” Lethira answered.

“So are they.” Serenya pointed past the trees. “The Amani broke the control fetishes and drove a Scourge column up the Scar. Ghouls, skeletons, two necromancers, at least one stitched brute. They struck the runestone web before my scouts could turn them. The western span failed.”

Falanaras reached toward the boundary with his trained senses. The runestone network trembled around a gap farther east, its currents frayed and lashing. Beyond that breach, necromantic power moved through Eversong in pulsing knots.
“How far?” Liadrin asked.

“Less than a league. Boundary wardens and a ranger patrol are delaying them near the old orchard road. Six of mine are on the eastern flank.” Serenya looked at the black-and-crimson ranks. Her eyes were filmed and cold, yet the attention behind them remained exact. “Whatever you have become, use it while there are living elves left to defend.”

Liadrin turned her mount. “Shield file with Theron. Strike file with Falanaras. The rest hold between them and recover the wounded. Rangers screen both flanks.” She looked once toward the south, where the Dead Scar cut through the hostile Ghostlands toward ruins no one held. “We fight inside Eversong. We close the breach after.”
No speech followed. The hawkstriders surged north.
The first corpse Falanaras saw wore a warden’s crimson cloak.

It lay beneath an apple tree whose spring blossoms had blackened in a single afternoon. Past it, the orchard road opened onto a low rise churned to mud. A dozen boundary defenders held the crest behind a failing ward. Ghouls clawed against its surface. Skeletons pressed through the gaps with rusted spears, and death bolts fell among the defenders in slow green arcs.

Behind the Scourge front came the abomination, huge enough to rise above the trees. Hooks swung from chains buried in its shoulders. Three mismatched arms dragged a butcher’s cleaver through the mud. A necromancer walked in its shadow, staff raised, feeding commands through a web of sickly light.

Falanaras saw the web before he saw the individual strands. Spellbreaker training separated the pressure into its parts: control lines, reinforcement knots, death magic drawn from charms tied along the brute’s spine. The structure was crude and strong. Breaking the necromancer alone might leave the creature raging without direction.
“Dismount!” he called.

The knights hit the ground at a run. Theron’s file reached the crest first. Five shields locked, and red-gold Light spread from one to the next. Their barrier struck the failing warden spell from behind and braced it. The two wards mingled badly, red-gold radiance grinding against blue arcane lines, but they held.
The nearest defenders stared for half a breath. Theron slammed his shield rim against the earth.
“Be surprised later,” he said. “Brace now.”
The wardens obeyed.
Liadrin’s ranseur swept forward. “Strike.”

Falanaras crossed through the barrier as Theron opened a narrow seam. The Light entered his sword at the first step. M’uru’s wounded music rose within the rush, and he gave the power a purpose before appetite could name one for him.

His first cut took a ghoul across the chest. Red-gold fire burst through dead flesh and burned along the bones beneath. The creature came apart before it reached the ground. Daric struck beside him with a heavy blade, crushing a skeleton’s breastbone in a flare bright enough to cast tree shadows. Two more knights widened the breach.

The effect on the Scourge was immediate. Holy fire clung to necromantic bindings. Sigils ruptured. Ghouls that had endured arrows and ordinary steel recoiled from wounds that continued consuming them. For years Falanaras had fought the undead with exhaustion as his closest companion. Now power moved through him with terrible abundance.
A death bolt came low from the right. His senses caught its current. He turned the sword, hooked the spell with the old motion of his training, and pulled.

Fel-green force thinned between his fingers. He took a bounded measure, twisted it away from its killing course, and drove the stolen magic into the mud. The ground burst beneath three skeletons. Before the spray fell, Falanaras was among them with his sword.

Light and mana answered different hungers in him. One carried M’uru’s cry. The other held the familiar bitterness of a hostile spell stripped for use. Neither absolved the hand taking it. Both kept the line alive.

Arrows passed over his shoulders. Lethira’s rangers fired from the orchard rows, each shot chosen to break knees, throats, and casting hands. Black-fletched Forsaken arrows answered from farther east. For several moments the two volleys crossed above the battlefield without any command joining them.
The abomination reached the crest.

Its cleaver struck Theron’s barrier. The impact flattened grass and drove every shield knight back a pace. One dropped to a knee. Light swelled around him in panic, spilling past the joined ward in bright, ragged sheets.
“Close it,” Theron ordered.
The knight’s eyes were wide. “It will break through.”
“Then give me the strength to stop it. Close your excess.”

Theron’s calm reached him where reassurance might have failed. The ragged flare narrowed. Theron caught it through the joined shields, gathered the current into a dense curve, and leaned into the next blow. Cleaver met radiance. This time the barrier held.
“Falanaras!” Liadrin called.

He was already moving. The necromantic web around the abomination tightened with every strike. Three knots pulsed beneath the stitched skin: one at the spine, one in the chest, one under the forward shoulder. The Light showed them as shadows within a brighter world.
Daric went left. Falanaras went right.

A hooked chain swept toward him. He ducked beneath it and cut upward through the creature’s lower arm. Holy fire filled the wound. Daric’s blade struck the shoulder knot from the other side. The binding snapped with a sound like wet rope. One of the abomination’s arms fell slack.
The brute roared. Its cleaver tore free of Theron’s ward and came down toward Falanaras.

A shield of red-gold Light appeared between them. It lasted less than a heartbeat. The cleaver shattered it, yet the delay let Falanaras roll clear. He came up on one knee and saw Theron behind the shield line, one arm extended through the gap.
“Adequate?” Theron called.
Falanaras drove his sword through the chest knot. “Improving.”

Radiance burst inside the abomination. Stitches blazed. The creature convulsed, struck blindly, and crushed two ghouls beneath its own feet. Liadrin’s ranseur entered the final knot at the spine. She released a single concentrated pulse. The binding vanished. The stitched brute sagged forward, its stolen parts surrendering to weight.
The victory lasted one breath.
Then a horn sounded from the eastern orchard. Three short notes. Serenya turned toward it before anyone else.
“My scouts are cut off.”

Through the trees, Falanaras caught movement: black cloaks among a knot of skeletons, ghouls closing from behind, another necromantic current hidden below the rise. The eastern Scourge flank had curled around the Forsaken position. Worse, it carried the stronger command line. The necromancer behind the abomination had been a decoy or a subordinate.
Lethira reached Serenya with an arrow nocked. “Can they withdraw?”

“No. The hollow behind them commands the eastern flank. If they run now, the whole line follows.” Serenya pointed toward a stand of white-barked trees beyond her trapped scouts. “Give us twenty breaths under cover. My scouts will expose the focus. When it breaks, we withdraw through the confusion.”
“And if you are wrong?” Lethira asked.
Serenya met her eyes. Rain ran across dead skin and gathered at her jaw without drawing a blink. “Then you lose twenty breaths and six Forsaken. If I am right, the whole host loses its spine.”

Their shared history stood between them: the ranger they had each been, the kingdom that had died around one and failed to bury the other, Sylvanas’s shadow over every word. Lethira’s face closed until only the field remained.
“Twenty,” she said. She turned to Falanaras. “Can you cover them?”
Twenty breaths. A low ward that preserved the scouts’ sight lines and took the death bolts where they were falling.
“Yes,” he said. “Bring two rangers to mark the edges. Daric, with me.”

They fought east through the orchard. Falanaras cut a path while Daric guarded his exposed side. Lethira’s arrows marked two trees at the edge of the trapped scouts’ position. Each shaft carried a blue ward-thread. Falanaras drove his sword into the mud between them and opened the Light.
Pain sang through him. The current pressed toward release.

A high, seamless wall would blind the scouts and diffuse strength across ground the Scourge was not striking. He built the ward low and angled, thickest beneath the falling death bolts. Daric added his current at the western edge. Two recovery knights reached them and anchored the other side. Red-gold planes joined between the marked trees, uneven as hammered metal and fitted to the retreat beneath them.
The first death bolt struck and spread green fire across the surface. The shield held.
“One,” Lethira counted.

Serenya ran beneath the cover. Her scouts moved with her, some limping, all still shooting. They did not flee north toward safety. They wheeled south and east, drawing the ghouls after them, peeling the Scourge flank away from the hidden hollow.
At eight breaths, a skeleton reached the shield’s end. Daric met it with his shoulder and smashed it against a tree.
At twelve, the hidden necromancer understood the maneuver. The command line tightened. Every ghoul in the eastern orchard turned at once.

At fifteen, the ward bowed so deeply that Falanaras saw the nearest death bolt through a handspan of red-gold fire. He opened the current wider and drove the added force into the failing span rather than across the whole barrier. Daric’s jaw clenched at the western anchor. Across the ward, one recovery knight’s arms shook as the reinforced planes brightened over the impact line, still low enough for the scouts to see their marks.
He held the strengthened ward against the next strike.
A black arrow rose from the hollow. It struck a branch above the necromancer’s concealment. The shaft carried a strip of white cloth.
“There,” Serenya shouted.
Lethira pivoted. Her bow bent to the ear. She did not look toward Serenya again. She trusted the mark.
The arrow vanished between the trees.

A robed figure staggered into view with the shaft buried beneath its jaw. The necromancer clawed at the fletching. Serenya’s second arrow struck its wrist. Her third entered the green crystal mounted within the bone frame behind it.
The focus cracked.

Falanaras felt the command line recoil through the entire host. Skeletons faltered in mid-stride. Ghouls spun toward the sudden absence behind them. The remaining necromancer near the road raised both hands, trying to gather the severed strands.
Liadrin reached him first.
Her ranseur passed through his staff and breastbone in one red-gold stroke. She wrenched the blade free and lifted it high.
“Advance.”

Theron’s shields moved as one. The wardens advanced behind them. With Serenya’s scouts clear and the command line broken, Falanaras tore his sword from the earth and let the rough ward fall. Exhaustion struck at once, followed by the returning ache of magical hunger. He accepted both. The Light had done what he asked of it, and M’uru had suffered for every measure.
The Blood Knights drove down the rise.

Their first field battle ended without ceremony. Theron’s shield crushed a ghoul against a broken cart. Daric split the last deathguard’s helm. Liadrin burned the remaining fetishes from the abomination’s corpse. Falanaras and Lethira fought back-to-back near the orchard wall, sword and bow choosing whatever survived the other. Serenya’s scouts came in from the flank and put black arrows into every undead creature that tried to crawl south.

One of the boundary defenders fell as the line moved. A Forsaken ranger caught him before he struck the ground. For an instant the living elf hung in gray arms, horror plain on his face. Then the dark ranger dragged him behind Theron’s shields and shouted for a healer.
A Blood Knight knelt beside them. Red-gold Light entered the wound while the Forsaken held the elf still.
No one named the strangeness. There was too much blood in the mud.
By dusk, the Scourge incursion had become rows of burning remains along the orchard road.

The rain stopped. Smoke climbed through the branches and turned the restored spring air bitter. Wardwrights arrived from the north with replacement stones and silver wire. Under guard, they began drawing the western span of the boundary closed. Each repaired line gave a low note that Falanaras felt in his teeth.

The wounded lay beneath orchard awnings. Blood Knights moved among them in black and crimson, closing wounds, easing shock, and learning how much Light a body could bear after terror had stripped away the discipline of a practice chamber. Their radiance made the scene beautiful from a distance. Up close, clenched jaws, shaking hands, and breaths held until each flare faded betrayed what the radiance cost at its source.
Theron sat on a fallen section of wall while Lethira stitched a cut above his ear.
“We have healers now,” he said.
“You have people who set practice posts on fire.” Lethira pulled the stitch tight. “Hold still.”

Falanaras leaned against the wall beside them. His arms felt hollow after the sustained ward. The ache of magical hunger had returned with exhaustion. He reached for the Light, took only enough to still the tremor, and let it go. M’uru’s pain lingered behind the rain-smoke bitterness in his mouth. He watched a Forsaken scout splint a ranger’s ankle while the ranger pretended to study the smoke.
“We would have buried twice as many without the order,” Theron said.

Falanaras knew what he meant: the shields, the healing, the way stolen Light had torn through creatures that had cost them blood for years. The judgment held no triumph, only the hard accounting of a soldier whose line had survived.
“Yes,” Falanaras said.
The answer did not require him to forget the source.

Near the fractured runestone, Serenya gathered her scouts. Two could still walk without help. One had lost an arm below the elbow and bound the stump with a strip torn from her own cloak. Liadrin ordered a recovery knight to offer healing once. The words came hard, as though forced through clenched teeth. When every Forsaken refused, relief crossed her face before she mastered it. She understood what they were. Her body still answered them as Scourge.

Lethira approached Serenya alone. The dark ranger held out the white cloth she had used to mark the hidden necromancer. An old Farstrider emblem had been embroidered at one corner, faded almost beyond recognition.
“You kept that,” Lethira said.
“It was useful.” Serenya’s ruined voice gave the word no warmth. She folded the cloth and returned it to a pouch. “Your judgment was sound.”
“So was yours.”
The words seemed to cost Lethira more than drawing the bow had. Serenya inclined her head. Neither reached across the distance between them.

Liadrin joined them at the boundary and stopped beyond easy reach. Her grip tightened on the ranseur. Red-gold Light kindled along its blade before she extinguished it, a reflex too swift to disguise. “There will be another incursion.”
“There is always another,” Serenya said.

“Then send warning to this line,” Liadrin said. Each word came clipped by an anger battle had not spent. “If the Scourge cross it, we will answer. Do not mistake that for welcome.” Her gaze stayed on Serenya’s dead face. “Today proved the method.”
Serenya looked past her to the Blood Knights among the wounded. Red-gold light rose and faded beneath the trees. “It proved several things.”
Liadrin’s jaw tightened. She offered no defense and no acknowledgment. Acceptance would have been too generous a name for her silence.

The repaired runestone span brightened. A curtain of faint blue force passed through the orchard from west to east, stirring smoke and dead leaves. South of it, the Ghostlands lay under gathering dark. Tranquillien remained a hostile ruin beyond sight. Deatholme still stood farther down the Scar. The day’s victory had reclaimed none of that ground.

Serenya’s scouts crossed through the boundary before the ward settled to full strength. The living elves watched them go. A few offered stiff gestures of acknowledgment. The Forsaken returned them without turning around.
Lethira stood beside Falanaras as Serenya disappeared among the blighted trees.
“Do not say anything thoughtful,” she murmured.
“I was going to ask whether you intended to keep pretending your hands were steady.”
She glanced at his hands. The magical tremor had eased, but the muscles still shook from strain now that battle discipline was loosening. “Sit down before you fall down.”
“That was almost concern.”
“You have been struck in the head repeatedly.”

Behind them, Liadrin called the Blood Knights to order. Fourteen had ridden south. Fourteen still stood, though several needed help to mount. Boundary defenders lined the road to watch them form. Awe, gratitude, and unease shared the same faces.

Falanaras took his place beside Theron. Blood darkened the new crimson edging of his tabard until cloth and stain became difficult to distinguish. His sword felt heavier than it had on the practice court. The Light still waited within reach, effective, coerced, and ready to answer again.

They had saved southern Eversong. They had held the boundary beside people many in Silvermoon regarded as monsters. Neither fact softened the other. Neither erased the captive beneath the city whose suffering had made their strength possible.
Liadrin looked down the line. Weariness had sharpened her face, but her voice carried across the orchard.
“We return north.”

The Blood Knights turned toward Silvermoon, leaving the restored ward at their backs and the hostile south beyond it. Their first victory followed them in the eyes of the living. M’uru’s cry followed in the Light.
